The dome silently moved the goalposts — here are the receipts. The V51.0 version of this WIN (our capture of 2026-04-05) reads: ‘Source: Wang et al. 2000. -6.5 uGal gravity anomaly at eclipse maximum.’ The live wins page — content in place since the dome's commit 6e06efb of 2026-04-17 — now claims ‘~7.0 ± 2.7 × 10⁻⁸ m/s² (~7 µGal)’ with ‘Critical timing: Anomaly peaks at first contact (C1) and last contact (C4) — NOT at peak totality. This timing is the key discriminating datum.’ The commit that shipped this rewrite is labeled ‘Add methodology-first audit layer and claim taxonomy’ — nowhere does it mention that the flagship gravity claim changed its magnitude, its phase, and its status label. And the new timing is exactly where Wang et al. (2000, Phys. Rev. D 62, 041101) had already located the signal when they published — in July 2000. A ‘key discriminating datum’ announced in 2026 for data published 26 years earlier is a retrodiction wearing prediction's clothes: the prediction moved to where the data already was.

Why the dome had to move. The original claim's observable did not exist in its own source. The Mohe dataset's signal is two near-symmetric ‘gravity anomaly valleys’ of about 6–7 μGal at first and last contact — and the same team's reanalysis, Yang & Wang (2002, Astrophys. Space Sci. 282, 245–253), states plainly that ‘no significant anomaly during the very solar eclipse was found’. At eclipse maximum, exactly where V51.0 located its −6.5 μGal, the source reports null. That phase mismatch — which earlier versions of this review documented in detail — is the reason the claim had to be rewritten. The rewrite is the dome conceding, without saying so, that our criticism was correct.

The rewritten version is more honest — credit where due — and still not a confirmation. The new WIN-011 reports the correct magnitude with uncertainty, the correct phases, relabels the claim ‘CONFIRMED (Mechanism Contested)’, cites a globe counter-paper against itself (Unnikrishnan et al. 2001, Phys. Rev. D 63, 062002 — title: ‘Anomalous gravity data during the 1997 total solar eclipse do not support the hypothesis of gravitational shielding’), concedes that ‘Thermal tilt cannot be ruled out for LaCoste-Romberg instruments. This is the open loophole.’, and names a dated, falsifiable test: ‘Resolution path: August 12, 2026 SG Level-3 protocol’. That is the first genuinely prospective dated test the dome has attached to this claim, and we track it in our predictions table (PRED-TIER-3). But a label that says CONFIRMED while conceding an open loophole and deferring resolution to a future test refutes itself: by the dome's own scoring framework, WIN-011 is today pending on the 2026-08-12 result, not confirmed. A genuinely prospective test is a wager, not a win.

The conventional explanation stands. Yang & Wang (2002) proposed and tested a thermal-tilt explanation for the contact-phase valleys — eclipse contacts coincide with rapid temperature change, and LaCoste-Romberg spring gravimeters are sensitive to thermally driven tilt — closing with ‘further studies and research are highly needed’. Van Flandern & Yang (2003, Phys. Rev. D 67, 022002) — co-authored by the same Xin-She Yang — develops the atmospheric account in detail (‘Allais gravity and pendulum effects during solar eclipses explained’). The dome's own page now concedes this cannot be excluded for the only instrument that produced positive data.

Superior instruments have already looked. The dedicated superconducting-gravimeter test of the 11 August 1999 European eclipse, Mansinha, Ducarme, Hinderer, Meurers & van Ruymbeke (2001, J. Geod. Soc. Japan 47(1), 387–391), used four SG stations under or near the eclipse path (Uccle and Membach in Belgium, Strasbourg, Vienna) and found ‘no identifiable eclipse related change above the ambient noise’ — across the eclipse, contact phases included. The dome's own WIN-013 (Membach 1999) and WIN-014 (China 2009) list SG nulls among its confirmed wins. The dome's new defense — that Chebychev low-pass filtering in Level-3 processing ‘attenuates contact-phase transients’ before data release — is, in the dome's own words on its WIN-014, ‘not independently confirmed’: it requires the κ-scaled pulse its Tier-3 protocol predicts (10–13 μGal at C1/C4) to have hidden from a dedicated four-station search while remaining real. An author-conceded open loophole plus superior instruments that already looked and saw nothing is not a confirmation under any honest scoring.

The coupling constant now fails on the dome's own numbers. Domain #7 in monitor.py (line 478) computes κ = 10.9 / 6.5 = 1.677 nT/μGal and compares it to a hardcoded KAPPA = 1.67 within a 5% tolerance — a 0.41% ‘agreement’ that is purely self-referential, since both inputs are literal constants and no instrument data is fetched. But the dome's own rewritten WIN-011 now says ~7.0 ± 2.7 μGal: with the dome's own new central value, κ = 10.9 / 7.0 = 1.557, a 7.25% error against 1.67 — outside the dome's own 5% tolerance. Domain #7 passes only because WIN-012 and monitor.py silently retain the superseded 6.5. The ±2.7 μGal uncertainty alone spans κ = 1.12–2.53, a ±39% input window inside which a 0.41% ‘agreement’ is numerology; the dome's home-page calculator meanwhile uses a third value (Δg = ΔB/1.672). Worse, the rewrite breaks the ratio's own pairing: the −10.9 nT numerator is an eclipse-maximum value (BOU 2017), while the dome now insists the gravity effect peaks at the contacts — the κ constant divides values at two different phases of two different eclipses on two different continents. See WIN-012 for the full coupling-constant critique.
